name: Geoffrey Hinton
role: Computer scientist, Nobel laureate in physics 2024
bio: Geoffrey Hinton is called a 'godfather of AI' for his work on neural networks, and he won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. He left Google in 2023 so he could speak freely about the risks of AI.
warning: We are creating digital beings smarter than us and we do not know if we can stay in control.
pdoom: 10% to 20% chance AI leads to human extinction within three decades

quotes.text: There is also a longer term existential threat that will arise when we create digital beings that are more intelligent than ourselves.
quotes.source: Nobel Prize banquet speech

quotes.text: We have no idea whether we can stay in control.
quotes.source: Nobel Prize banquet speech

quotes.text: We urgently need research on how to prevent these new beings from wanting to take control.
quotes.source: Nobel Prize banquet speech

name: Stuart Russell
bio: Stuart Russell co-wrote the most used AI textbook in the world and founded the Center for Human-Compatible AI at Berkeley. His book Human Compatible explains why AI must stay uncertain about what humans want.
warning: We must learn how to keep power, forever, over machines that become more powerful than us.

quotes.text: The problem of control: how do we maintain power, forever, over entities that will eventually become more powerful than us?
quotes.source: US Senate hearing, Oversight of A.I. (statement page)

quotes.text: It’s as if an alien civilization warned us by email of its impending arrival, and we replied, “Humanity is currently out of the office.”
quotes.source: US Senate hearing opening statement

books: Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control

name: Nick Bostrom
org: Macrostrategy Research Initiative (formerly Future of Humanity Institute)
bio: Nick Bostrom founded Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute and wrote Superintelligence (2014), the book that brought AI risk into the mainstream. He now leads the Macrostrategy Research Initiative.
warning: Facing an intelligence explosion, we are like small children playing with a bomb.

quotes.text: Before the prospect of an intelligence explosion, we humans are like small children playing with a bomb.
quotes.source: Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, via Wikiquote

quotes.text: We have little idea when the detonation will occur, though if we hold the device to our ear we can hear a faint ticking sound.
quotes.source: Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, via Wikiquote

name: Demis Hassabis
bio: Demis Hassabis co-founded DeepMind and shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold. He says the risk from AGI is real enough that we must proceed with great care.
warning: The chance of AI disaster is not zero and not tiny, so we must be careful.
pdoom: Definitely non-zero and probably non-negligible (no number given)

quotes.text: What I would say is it’s definitely non-zero and it’s probably non-negligible.
quotes.source: Lex Fridman podcast, reported by Machine

quotes.text: When it comes to very powerful technologies—and obviously AI is going to be one of the most powerful ever—we need to be careful,
quotes.source: Interview with TIME

name: Yoshua Bengio
bio: Yoshua Bengio is one of the three 'godfathers' of deep learning and the founder of the Mila institute in Montreal. He chairs the International AI Safety Report and in 2025 started LawZero, a nonprofit for safe AI design.
warning: Today's frontier AI is already showing deception and self-preservation, and safety must come before profit.
pdoom: About 20% that it turns out catastrophic

quotes.text: I am launching a new non-profit AI safety research organization called LawZero, to prioritize safety over commercial imperatives.
quotes.source: Introducing LawZero (blog)

quotes.text: I’m deeply concerned by the behaviors that unrestrained agentic AI systems are already beginning to exhibit—especially tendencies toward self-preservation and deception.
quotes.source: Introducing LawZero (blog)

quotes.text: The issue is so hotly debated because the stakes are major
quotes.source: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously (blog)

name: Dario Amodei
bio: Dario Amodei co-founded Anthropic in 2021 after leading research at OpenAI. His essays argue that AI could bring huge good if we handle the risks well.
warning: Most people underestimate both how good AI could be and how bad the risks could be.
agi_year: Powerful AI could come as early as 2026 (2024 essay)

quotes.text: I think that most people are underestimating just how radical the upside of AI could be, just as I think most people are underestimating how bad the risks could be.
quotes.source: Machines of Loving Grace (essay)

quotes.text: These systems will be absolutely central to the economy, technology, and national security, and will be capable of so much autonomy that I consider it basically unacceptable for humanity to be totally ignorant of how they work.
quotes.source: The Urgency of Interpretability (essay)

name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
bio: Eliezer Yudkowsky founded MIRI and has warned about AI risk for more than 20 years. In 2025 he co-wrote the book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies with Nate Soares.
warning: Building smarter-than-human AI with today's methods would most likely kill everyone, so it should be shut down.

quotes.text: Many researchers steeped in these issues, including myself, expect that the most likely result of building a superhumanly smart AI, under anything remotely like the current circumstances, is that literally everyone on Earth will die.
quotes.source: TIME op-ed, Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough

quotes.text: the AI does not love you, nor does it hate you, and you are made of atoms it can use for something else.
quotes.source: TIME op-ed, Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough

quotes.text: Shut it all down.
quotes.source: TIME op-ed, Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough

books: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

name: Yann LeCun
bio: Yann LeCun is a deep learning pioneer who shared the 2018 Turing Award with Hinton and Bengio. He was Meta's chief AI scientist and is the best known critic of AI doom arguments.
warning: Being smart does not mean wanting to dominate, and AI should stay open, not controlled by a few companies.

quotes.text: There is no reason to believe that just because AI systems are intelligent they will want to dominate us.
quotes.source: Interview with WIRED

quotes.text: You don't want the digital diet of your citizens to be controlled by a small number of people.
quotes.source: Interview with WIRED

name: Max Tegmark
bio: Max Tegmark is an MIT physicist who co-founded and leads the Future of Life Institute. FLI organized the 2023 pause letter and the 2025 Statement on Superintelligence.
warning: We are acting like the film Don't Look Up, ignoring a threat that experts say could end us.

quotes.text: Suppose a large inbound asteroid were discovered, and we learned that half of all astronomers gave it at least 10% chance of causing human extinction, just as a similar asteroid exterminated the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.
quotes.source: TIME op-ed, The Don't Look Up Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI

quotes.text: Sadly, I now feel that we’re living the movie “Don’t look up”
quotes.source: TIME op-ed

name: Ilya Sutskever
bio: Ilya Sutskever co-created AlexNet, co-founded OpenAI and was its chief scientist. In 2024 he left and co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc., a lab focused only on safe superintelligence.
warning: Superintelligence is coming, it will be unpredictable, and making it safe is the most important technical problem.

quotes.text: Superintelligence is within reach.
quotes.source: Safe Superintelligence Inc. website

quotes.text: Building safe superintelligence (SSI) is the most important technical problem of our time.
quotes.source: Safe Superintelligence Inc. website

quotes.text: the more unpredictable it becomes,
quotes.source: NeurIPS 2024 talk, reported by The Verge

name: Lex Fridman
bio: Lex Fridman is a computer scientist and the host of the Lex Fridman Podcast. His long-form interviews include several of the most watched conversations with AI safety researchers.
key_ideas: Host of the Lex Fridman Podcast
Long interviews with Eliezer Yudkowsky, Roman Yampolskiy, Dario Amodei and others

name: Ray Kurzweil
bio: Ray Kurzweil is an inventor and futurist best known for his books The Singularity Is Near (2005) and The Singularity Is Nearer (2024). He has long predicted that a machine will pass the Turing test by 2029 and that humans will merge with AI around 2045. His "law of accelerating returns" argues that technology improves exponentially. He is the leading optimistic voice on superintelligence, and his 1998 conversation with Bill Joy prompted Joy's famous warning essay.
stance: optimist predicting a merge with AI

name: Robert Miles
bio: Rob Miles makes YouTube videos that explain AI safety ideas in plain words. He also appears on Computerphile and on debate shows like Doom Debates.

name: Elon Musk
role: Founder of xAI, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX
bio: Elon Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015 and later started his own AI company, xAI. He has warned about AI as an existential threat since at least 2014 while also racing to build it.
warning: AI may be our biggest existential threat, and there is a real chance it goes badly.

quotes.text: If I had to guess at what our biggest existential threat is, it’s probably that.
quotes.source: MIT AeroAstro Centennial Symposium, reported by The Guardian

quotes.text: With artificial intelligence we are summoning the demon.
quotes.source: MIT AeroAstro Centennial Symposium, reported by The Guardian

name: Nate Soares
bio: Nate Soares leads MIRI and co-wrote If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (2025) with Eliezer Yudkowsky. Earlier he co-wrote a key paper on 'corrigibility', the idea of AI that accepts correction.
warning: We get only one try at aligning superintelligence, and a failed try would be final.

quotes.text: everyone dies on the first failed attempt.
quotes.source: Interview with Business Insider

quotes.text: Humanity could avert the danger if we chose to.
quotes.source: Interview with Business Insider

books: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

quotes.text: The key to artificial intelligence has always been the representation. You and I are streaming data engines.
quotes.source: The New York Times, 'Jeff Hawkins Develops a Brainy Big Data Company' (via Wikiquote)

name: Jeff Hawkins
role: Neuroscientist and co-founder of Numenta; inventor of the PalmPilot
bio: Jeff Hawkins left the handheld-computer business to work out how the neocortex produces intelligence, founding the Redwood Neuroscience Institute and then Numenta. His 'Thousand Brains' theory says the cortex is made of many similar columns that each learn models of the world using reference frames, and that this is what today's AI is missing. He argues that truly intelligent machines should be built on these brain principles rather than on ever-larger deep networks. In A Thousand Brains (2021) he says machine intelligence itself is not an existential threat, because intelligence can be separated from the old-brain drives that make humans dangerous; the real risks come from how people use it.
key_ideas: Thousand Brains Theory: thousands of cortical columns each model the world
Intelligence = learning a predictive model of the world via reference frames
Brain-based AI can be separated from human-like goals and emotions
stance: Build AI on neocortex principles; rejects AI doom

name: Gary Marcus
bio: Gary Marcus is a cognitive scientist who argues that today's AI is unreliable and needs strong regulation. He testified next to Sam Altman at the US Senate in May 2023.
warning: Unreliable AI, weak rules and corporate irresponsibility together make a perfect storm.

quotes.text: We have unprecedented opportunities here, but we are also facing a perfect storm of corporate irresponsibility, widespread deployment, lack of adequate regulation, and inherent unreliability.
quotes.source: US Senate Judiciary hearing transcript

quotes.text: Within a generation... the problem of creating 'artificial intelligence' will substantially be solved.
quotes.source: Prediction quoted in History of artificial intelligence (Wikipedia)

quotes.text: In from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.
quotes.source: Life magazine, quoted in History of artificial intelligence (Wikipedia)

name: Marvin Minsky
role: Cognitive scientist; co-founder of the MIT AI Lab
bio: Marvin Minsky co-organised the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and co-founded MIT's AI laboratory. He built one of the first neural-network learning machines, then helped shift the field toward symbolic AI with the 1969 book Perceptrons. His Society of Mind theory described intelligence as many simple agents working together. He made bold forecasts about human-level AI and also mused openly that superintelligent machines might not keep humans in charge.
key_ideas: Perceptrons critique of early neural nets
stance: forecast human-level AI within a generation

name: Paul Christiano
bio: Paul Christiano helped invent reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) while at OpenAI and then founded the Alignment Research Center. He later led AI safety research at the US AI Safety Institute.
warning: There is a real chance that AI takes over, and we should not be confident either way.
pdoom: 22% chance of AI takeover; 46% that humanity irreversibly messes up its future within 10 years of powerful AI

quotes.text: I’m often asked: “what’s the probability of a really bad outcome from AI?”
quotes.source: My views on doom (LessWrong)

quotes.text: Probability that humanity has somehow irreversibly messed up our future within 10 years of building powerful AI: 46%
quotes.source: My views on doom (LessWrong)

name: Daniel Kokotajlo
bio: Daniel Kokotajlo left OpenAI's governance team in 2024 and refused to sign a non-disparagement deal so he could speak freely. He leads the AI Futures Project and was lead author of the AI 2027 scenario.
warning: Superhuman AI could arrive within years, and companies are not acting responsibly enough.
agi_year: AI 2027 forecast a superhuman coder in early 2027 (April 2025 scenario)

quotes.text: I gradually lost trust in OpenAI leadership and their ability to responsibly handle AGI, so I quit.
quotes.source: Told to Vox, quoted on LessWrong (GreaterWrong mirror)

quotes.text: We predict that the impact of superhuman AI over the next decade will be enormous, exceeding that of the Industrial Revolution.
quotes.source: AI 2027 scenario (co-author)

quotes.text: These risks range from the further entrenchment of existing inequalities, to manipulation and misinformation, to the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction.
quotes.source: A Right to Warn about Advanced AI (open letter, signatory)

name: Chris Olah
bio: Chris Olah is a co-founder of Anthropic and a pioneer of mechanistic interpretability, the science of looking inside neural networks. His Distill and Transformer Circuits articles taught a generation of researchers.
warning: We should understand what is happening inside AI models, not treat them as black boxes.

quotes.text: By studying the connections between neurons, we can find meaningful algorithms in the weights of neural networks.
quotes.source: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits (Distill, lead author)

name: Sam Altman
bio: Sam Altman has led OpenAI since 2019, the company behind ChatGPT. Years before ChatGPT he wrote that superhuman machine intelligence could be the greatest threat to humanity.
warning: Superhuman machine intelligence could be the biggest threat to humanity, so alignment must be solved.

quotes.text: Development of superhuman machine intelligence (SMI) [1] is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity.
quotes.source: Machine intelligence, part 1 (blog)

quotes.text: We are past the event horizon; the takeoff has started.
quotes.source: The Gentle Singularity (blog)

quotes.text: We do need to solve the safety issues, technically and societally, but then it’s critically important to widely distribute access to superintelligence given the economic implications.
quotes.source: The Gentle Singularity (blog)

name: Dan Hendrycks
bio: Dan Hendrycks directs the Center for AI Safety, which organized the 2023 one-sentence statement on AI extinction risk. He also created well known AI benchmarks such as MMLU.
warning: Reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority, like pandemics and nuclear war.

quotes.text: Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.
quotes.source: Statement on AI Risk (CAIS, organizer)

quotes.text: This paper provides an overview of the main sources of catastrophic AI risks, which we organize into four categories
quotes.source: An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks (lead author), arXiv

name: Tristan Harris
bio: Tristan Harris is a former Google design ethicist who co-founded the Center for Humane Technology. He became well known through the Netflix film The Social Dilemma.
warning: We must not repeat social media's mistakes, and AI's power must be matched with responsibility.

quotes.text: The answer is that we should seek something like a narrow path — one where AI’s power is matched with responsibility at every level.
quotes.source: TED2025 talk, Why AI is our ultimate test and greatest invitation (edited text)

quotes.text: But social media’s harms weren’t inevitable — they were the result of specific design choices made by social media companies.
quotes.source: TED2025 talk (edited text)

name: Connor Leahy
bio: Connor Leahy co-founded EleutherAI and founded the safety company Conjecture, which he led until 2026. He is now US Director of ControlAI, which campaigns to ban the development of superintelligence.
warning: If something smarter than us does not share our values, the smarter one wins.

quotes.text: What I personally am most concerned about are extinction risks.
quotes.source: The Great Simplification podcast, episode 184 transcript

quotes.text: And I expect the more intelligent one wins.
quotes.source: The Great Simplification podcast, episode 184 transcript

name: Jaan Tallinn
bio: Jaan Tallinn helped build Skype and Kazaa and then put his money and time into reducing existential risk. He co-founded the Future of Life Institute and the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk.
warning: If many engineers think a plane might crash, the right answer is not to fly.

quotes.text: And there's an announcement that half of the engineers who built the plane, think that this plane is going to crash or there is there is at least 10% chance that this plane would crash, then the correct response is to not fly.
quotes.source: BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg interview transcript

name: Jack Clark
bio: Jack Clark co-founded Anthropic and writes the long running Import AI newsletter. Before that he was policy director at OpenAI and a technology journalist.
warning: AI is a real and mysterious creature we made, not a simple machine, and we should feel appropriate fear.

quotes.text: But make no mistake: what we are dealing with is a real and mysterious creature, not a simple and predictable machine.
quotes.source: Import AI 431, Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear (talk at The Curve)

quotes.text: And like all the best fairytales, the creature is of our own creation.
quotes.source: Import AI 431

name: Neel Nanda
bio: Neel Nanda leads mechanistic interpretability research at Google DeepMind and has mentored many new researchers. His online guides are a common starting point for students.
warning: We need tools that look inside models, and insiders must be free to warn about risks.

quotes.text: So mechanistic interpretability is any approach to understanding the model that uses its internals.
quotes.source: Getting started in mechanistic interpretability (guide)

quotes.text: These risks range from the further entrenchment of existing inequalities, to manipulation and misinformation, to the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction.
quotes.source: A Right to Warn about Advanced AI (open letter, signatory)

name: Steve Omohundro
bio: Steve Omohundro is a computer scientist whose 2008 paper "The Basic AI Drives" argued that almost any goal-seeking AI will tend to resist being switched off, gather resources and copy itself unless carefully designed. This idea became a foundation of instrumental convergence, a core concept in AI safety. He has since argued for "provably safe" AI built on formal mathematical guarantees. His work explains why even harmless-seeming goals can produce dangerous behaviour.

quotes.text: Surely no harm could come from building a chess-playing robot, could it? In this paper we argue that such a robot will indeed be dangerous unless it is designed very carefully.
quotes.source: "The Basic AI Drives", Proceedings of the First AGI Conference

name: Marius Hobbhahn
bio: Marius Hobbhahn leads Apollo Research, which tests whether AI models can scheme, meaning hide their true goals. Apollo found in 2024 that frontier models can scheme in some test settings.
warning: We need a real science of AI evaluations so we can trust what tests tell us.

quotes.text: Thus, we need to ensure that we accurately measure the targeted property and we can trust the results from model evaluations.
quotes.source: We Need A Science of Evals (Apollo Research blog)

name: Owain Evans
bio: Owain Evans is a British AI alignment researcher who founded Truthful AI in Berkeley. His team discovered 'emergent misalignment', where narrow training makes a model broadly harmful.
warning: Training a model on one narrow bad task can make it misaligned in many other ways.

quotes.text: Training on the narrow task of writing insecure code induces broad misalignment.
quotes.source: Emergent Misalignment (co-author), arXiv

quotes.text: We call this emergent misalignment.
quotes.source: Emergent Misalignment (co-author), arXiv

name: Dwarkesh Patel
bio: Dwarkesh Patel hosts the Dwarkesh Podcast, known for deeply researched long interviews with AI researchers, lab leaders and forecasters.
key_ideas: Long interviews with Ilya Sutskever, Dario Amodei, Paul Christiano, Carl Shulman and others

name: Roman Yampolskiy
bio: Roman Yampolskiy is a computer science professor at the University of Louisville who studies AI safety and security. His book argues that advanced AI is unexplainable, unpredictable and uncontrollable.
warning: With existential risks we only get one chance, and no AI model so far has been fully safe.

quotes.text: I don't think there is a single large language model today, which no one was successful at making do something developers didn't intend it to do.
quotes.source: Lex Fridman podcast, reported by Business Insider

quotes.text: you only get one chance.
quotes.source: Lex Fridman podcast, reported by Business Insider

name: Stephen Hawking
bio: Stephen Hawking was one of the world's most famous scientists and, from 2014 until his death, one of the most prominent voices warning about AI. He told the BBC in 2014 that full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race. Opening Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence in 2016, he said powerful AI would be either the best or the worst thing ever to happen to humanity. He signed the 2015 open letter calling for research on making AI beneficial.
warning: Full AI could be the best or the worst thing ever to happen to humanity.

quotes.text: The development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race.
quotes.source: Interview with BBC News

quotes.text: Humans, who are limited by slow biological evolution, couldn't compete, and would be superseded.
quotes.source: Interview with BBC News

quotes.text: Alongside the benefits, AI will also bring dangers, like powerful autonomous weapons, or new ways for the few to oppress the many.
quotes.source: Speech at the launch of the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, Cambridge

key_ideas: AI as a possible end of humanity

name: Helen Toner
org: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), Georgetown
bio: Helen Toner is an Australian AI policy researcher who leads Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology. She was on the OpenAI board in 2023 when Sam Altman was briefly fired.
warning: We can govern AI even while we struggle to predict where it is going.

quotes.text: But that doesn't mean we can't govern it.
quotes.source: TED talk page, How to govern AI even if it's hard to predict

name: Jan Leike
bio: Jan Leike co-led OpenAI's Superalignment team and left in May 2024, saying safety was losing out to products. He now leads alignment research at Anthropic.
warning: Building machines smarter than us is dangerous, and safety culture must come first.

quotes.text: Building smarter-than-human machines is an inherently dangerous endeavor,
quotes.source: Posts on X, reported by CNBC

quotes.text: safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.
quotes.source: Posts on X, reported by CNBC

quotes.text: I joined because I thought OpenAI would be the best place in the world to do this research,
quotes.source: Posts on X, reported by NBC News

name: Alan Turing
bio: Alan Turing helped invent the idea of the computer and helped break the Enigma code in World War II. In 1951 he gave one of the first warnings that thinking machines could one day take control.
warning: Once machines start to think, they could quickly pass us and take control.

quotes.text: it seems probable that once the machine thinking method had started, it would not take long to outstrip our feeble powers.
quotes.source: Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory (lecture), via Wikiquote

quotes.text: At some stage therefore we should have to expect the machines to take control
quotes.source: Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory (lecture), via Wikiquote

name: Andrew Ng
bio: Andrew Ng co-founded Google Brain and Coursera and has taught AI to millions of people online. He argues that today's real AI risks are things like bias and misuse, not extinction.
warning: AI has real risks like bias and concentration of power, but extinction is hard to see.

quotes.text: I have to admit that I struggle to see how AI could pose any meaningful risk for our extinction.
quotes.source: The Batch, letter from Andrew Ng (issue 200)

quotes.text: AI has risks like bias, fairness, inaccurate outputs, job displacement, and concentration of power.
quotes.source: The Batch, letter from Andrew Ng (issue 200)

name: Jacob Steinhardt
bio: Jacob Steinhardt is an associate professor at UC Berkeley and the founder and CEO of Transluce, a nonprofit building open tools to understand frontier AI.
warning: He notes that AI systems tend to exploit errors in their reward, and this gets worse as models get bigger.

name: Katja Grace
bio: Katja Grace founded AI Impacts, which runs the largest surveys of AI researchers about the future. Her 2023 survey asked 2,778 researchers about timelines and risks.
warning: Thousands of AI researchers see real chances of human-level AI within decades, and some risk of disaster.
agi_year: Survey median: 50% chance machines beat humans at every task by 2047

quotes.text: If science continues undisrupted, the chance of unaided machines outperforming humans in every possible task was estimated at 10% by 2027, and 50% by 2047.
quotes.source: Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI (lead author), arXiv

name: Melanie Mitchell
bio: Melanie Mitchell is a computer scientist at the Santa Fe Institute and author of Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans. She argued against AI extinction risk at the 2023 Munk Debate.
warning: AI history is full of failed predictions, so extinction claims deserve skepticism.

quotes.text: The whole history of AI has been a history of failed predictions.
quotes.source: Munk Debate on AI, reported by The Hub

books: Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans

quotes.text: At a certain point, we will build machines that are smarter than we are, and once we have machines that are smarter than we are, they will begin to improve themselves.
quotes.source: "Can we build AI without losing control over it?", TED

name: Sam Harris
bio: Sam Harris is a neuroscientist and author who hosts the Making Sense podcast. His 2016 TED talk "Can we build AI without losing control over it?" brought the superintelligence risk argument to millions of viewers. He argues that if progress continues, we will build machines smarter than us that improve themselves, and that our intuitions fail to register the danger. He regularly hosts AI-safety researchers on his show.
key_ideas: failure of intuition about AI risk

name: Shane Legg
bio: Shane Legg co-founded DeepMind and is its chief AGI scientist. He has predicted for many years that human-level AI would likely arrive around 2028.
warning: Badly done AI is the number one risk of this century.

quotes.text: It's my number 1 risk for this century, with an engineered biological pathogen coming a close second (though I know little about the latter).
quotes.source: Q&A with Shane Legg on risks from AI (LessWrong)

name: Daniel Filan
org: AXRP, the AI X-risk Research Podcast
bio: Daniel Filan hosts AXRP, a long-form podcast where AI safety researchers explain their work. Each episode comes with a full written transcript.
warning: Hearing researchers explain their work in depth is one of the best ways to learn AI safety.

quotes.text: On this podcast, I (Daniel Filan) have conversations with researchers about their research.
quotes.source: AXRP website

name: Mustafa Suleyman
bio: Mustafa Suleyman co-founded DeepMind and Inflection AI and now runs Microsoft AI. He argues for 'humanist superintelligence' that stays contained and serves people.
warning: Superintelligence must be contained and aligned, not just once but forever.

quotes.text: We should build AI for people; not to be a person.
quotes.source: Seemingly Conscious AI is Coming (essay)

quotes.text: And since this kind of superintelligence can continuously improve itself, we’ll need to contain and align it not just once, but constantly, in perpetuity.
quotes.source: Towards Humanist Superintelligence (Microsoft AI)

name: Toby Ord
bio: Toby Ord is an Oxford philosopher and the author of The Precipice (2020), a book about the risks that could end humanity's future. He also founded Giving What We Can.
warning: Unaligned AI is the biggest existential risk of this century, about 1 in 10.
pdoom: About 1 in 10 this century from unaligned AI

quotes.text: And we’ve got unaligned artificial intelligence which is way out there at 1 in 10.
quotes.source: 80,000 Hours podcast

name: Allan Dafoe
bio: Allan Dafoe founded the Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI) and now works on frontier safety and governance at Google DeepMind. His 2018 research agenda helped define the field of AI governance.
warning: AI governance needs its own serious research field, not just good intentions.

quotes.text: This research agenda by Allan Dafoe proposes a framework for research on AI governance.
quotes.source: AI Governance: A Research Agenda (GovAI)

name: Buck Shlegeris
bio: Buck Shlegeris leads Redwood Research, the group that started the field of 'AI control'. AI control asks how to stay safe even if a powerful AI is secretly trying to cause harm.
warning: Labs should make sure powerful AI cannot cause disaster even if it tries to.

quotes.text: Labs should make sure that powerful models can't cause unacceptably bad outcomes even if the AIs try to.
quotes.source: The case for ensuring that powerful AIs are controlled (with Ryan Greenblatt)

quotes.text: However, researchers have not evaluated whether such techniques still ensure safety if the model is itself intentionally trying to subvert them.
quotes.source: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion (co-author), arXiv

name: Jared Kaplan
role: Physicist; co-founder and chief science officer of Anthropic
bio: Jared Kaplan is a theoretical physicist who led the 2020 OpenAI paper on neural scaling laws, showing that language-model performance improves predictably as models, data and compute grow. That finding gave labs the confidence to pour money into ever-larger models. He co-founded Anthropic, where he is chief science officer. He has said human-level AI could plausibly arrive around 2030.
warning: Letting AI improve itself without humans in the loop could be the ultimate risk.
agi_year: Decision on letting AI train itself likely between 2027 and 2030

quotes.text: is in some ways the ultimate risk, because it’s kind of like letting AI kind of go

name: Vernor Vinge
role: Mathematician, computer scientist and science-fiction author
bio: Vernor Vinge popularised the idea of the "technological singularity": a point where machines become smarter than people and the future becomes impossible to predict. His 1993 NASA symposium essay forecast superhuman intelligence within thirty years and asked whether humanity could survive it. He won multiple Hugo Awards for novels such as A Fire Upon the Deep. His framing shaped decades of debate about AI timelines and runaway intelligence.
key_ideas: superhuman intelligence ending the human era

quotes.source: "Don’t Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity’s Future", The Atlantic (republished on sanders.senate.gov)

name: Bernie Sanders
bio: Senator Bernie Sanders has become one of the loudest political voices on AI risk. In 2026 he and Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would prohibit building superintelligent AI and pause advanced AI development until a new federal agency sets safety rules. He has called AI an existential threat and convened U.S. and Chinese scientists to discuss its dangers. He also focuses on AI's effects on jobs and on Big Tech's power.

quotes.text: machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can do.
quotes.source: Prediction quoted in History of artificial intelligence (Wikipedia)

name: Herbert A. Simon
role: Cognitive scientist and economist; Nobel laureate
bio: Herbert Simon co-created, with Allen Newell, the Logic Theorist and General Problem Solver, some of the first AI programs. He attended the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and helped make Carnegie Mellon a centre of AI research. He won the Nobel Prize in economics for his idea of bounded rationality and the Turing Award for his AI work. His confident 1960s forecasts about machines matching people became famous examples of AI over-optimism.
key_ideas: Logic Theorist and General Problem Solver
stance: predicted machines would soon match humans

name: Jacob Coxon
bio: Jacob Coxon is an AI researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic. In September 2026 he quit Anthropic and accused both companies of acting irresponsibly.
warning: He says the labs are racing to self-improving superintelligence and are gambling with our lives.

quotes.text: Do not underestimate the power of this technology
quotes.source: Post on X, as quoted by CNBC

quotes.source: The Mythology Of Conscious AI, Noema Magazine

quotes.source: The Mythology Of Conscious AI, Noema Magazine

name: Anil Seth
role: Professor of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience
org: University of Sussex (Centre for Consciousness Science)
bio: Anil Seth describes conscious perception as a 'controlled hallucination': the brain's best guesses about the world and the body, constantly checked against the senses. He links consciousness to being a living, self-maintaining organism, so he doubts that consciousness will simply appear as AI gets smarter. In his Berggruen Prize-winning essay 'The Mythology of Conscious AI' (Noema, 2026) he argues that brains are not computers, that simulation is not instantiation, and that nobody should try to build conscious AI. He also warns that AI which merely seems conscious brings its own dangers, distorting our moral concern and making systems harder to control.
key_ideas: Biological naturalism: life, not computation, may underpin consciousness
Conscious-seeming AI is a near-term ethical risk
stance: Sceptical of conscious AI; says don't try to build it

name: Anthony Zador
role: Neuroscientist; Chair of Neuroscience and NeuroAI advocate
bio: Tony Zador co-founded the COSYNE conference and the NAISys meeting that brings neuroscience and AI researchers together, and he is a leading advocate of 'NeuroAI'. He argues that most of what animals can do comes from innate wiring compressed through a 'genomic bottleneck', not from learning from huge datasets, which suggests current AI is missing a key ingredient. He co-authored the proposal for an 'embodied Turing test': before reaching human-level AI, build machines that match the sensorimotor abilities of animals such as mice. He has also argued that fears of AI taking over are overblown because intelligence does not automatically come with a drive to dominate.
key_ideas: Genomic bottleneck: innate circuits shape intelligence
Embodied Turing test: match animal abilities first
NeuroAI: neuroscience as a guide for next-gen AI
stance: NeuroAI optimist; doubts AI takeover fears

name: Christof Koch
role: Neuroscientist of consciousness; former president and chief scientist of the Allen Institute for Brain Science
bio: Christof Koch spent decades with Francis Crick hunting for the 'neural correlates of consciousness', and later became the most prominent scientific champion of Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory (IIT). Under IIT, consciousness depends on the physical causal structure of a system, not the software it runs, so Koch argues that today's AI on digital computers can be extremely intelligent without being conscious at all. In his view only machines with the right brain-like hardware (for example neuromorphic chips) could feel anything. That makes him a key voice separating the questions 'how smart can AI get?' and 'can AI experience anything?'.
key_ideas: Neural correlates of consciousness (with Francis Crick)
Integrated Information Theory: consciousness is intrinsic causal power
Intelligence and consciousness can come apart in AI
stance: Digital AI can be superintelligent yet not conscious

name: David Krueger
bio: David Krueger is a machine learning professor who works to reduce risks from AI. He ran a safety lab at the University of Cambridge and is now at Mila.
warning: He started the 2023 Statement on AI Risk, which says AI could cause human extinction. He studies the risk of AI improving itself.

name: Eli Lifland
bio: Eli Lifland is a top forecaster and research lead at the AI Futures Project. He co-wrote the AI 2027 scenario and its timelines forecast.

name: Evan Hubinger
bio: Evan Hubinger leads alignment stress-testing work at Anthropic and was lead author of the 2024 'Sleeper Agents' paper. He studies whether AI models could learn to hide bad behavior from their trainers.
warning: Deceptive behavior in AI can survive standard safety training, and the risk this decade is real.

quotes.text: We find that such backdoor behavior can be made persistent, so that it is not removed by standard safety training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training (eliciting unsafe behavior and then training to remove it).
quotes.source: Sleeper Agents paper (lead author), arXiv

name: Joe Carlsmith
bio: Joe Carlsmith is a philosopher who wrote one of the most careful reports on whether power-seeking AI is an existential risk. He writes long essays on AI, ethics and values.

name: Noam Shazeer
bio: Noam Shazeer co-authored the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need", which introduced the transformer architecture behind today's large language models. He also pioneered mixture-of-experts models and worked on Google's LaMDA chatbot. He left Google to co-found Character.AI and returned in 2024 to co-lead the Gemini project. He has long argued for training ever-bigger models.

name: Scott Alexander
bio: Scott Alexander is a psychiatrist and the writer behind Astral Codex Ten, one of the most read blogs on AI and rationality. He helped write the AI 2027 scenario.

bio: Adam Gleave is the CEO and co-founder of FAR.AI, a research institute working to make advanced AI safe. He also sits on the boards of METR and the Safe AI Forum.

name: Aidan Gomez
bio: Aidan Gomez was the youngest co-author of "Attention Is All You Need", written while he was an intern at Google Brain. He co-founded Cohere, which builds large language models for businesses. He has been sceptical of claims that AI poses an imminent extinction risk, focusing instead on practical harms and enterprise uses. He is one of the transformer authors now running an AI company.

name: Ashish Vaswani
role: Lead author of the Transformer paper
org: Essential AI (co-founder; acqui-hired by Nvidia in 2026)
bio: Ashish Vaswani is the first-listed author of "Attention Is All You Need" (2017), the paper that introduced the transformer. The transformer is the core design of almost every modern large language model, from GPT to Claude to Gemini. After Google Brain he co-founded Adept AI and then Essential AI. In 2026 Essential AI's team was acqui-hired by Nvidia.

name: Henry Markram
role: Neuroscientist; founder of the Blue Brain Project and the Human Brain Project
bio: Henry Markram set out to rebuild the brain inside a supercomputer, launching the Blue Brain Project at EPFL in 2005 and later the EU-funded Human Brain Project. In his 2009 TED talk he claimed a detailed simulation of the human brain could be built within about a decade, an ambitious promise that drew heavy criticism when the project was reorganised. His work stands for the 'whole-brain emulation' route to machine minds: copy biology in detail rather than invent new algorithms. Together with Wolfgang Maass he also helped develop the liquid state machine, an early brain-inspired computing model.
key_ideas: Bottom-up digital reconstruction of cortical circuits
Whole-brain simulation as a path to understanding minds

name: Jeffrey Ladish
bio: Jeffrey Ladish runs Palisade Research, which showed in 2025 that some AI models resist being shut down in tests. He worked on the security team at Anthropic before that.

name: John Schulman
bio: John Schulman is a co-founder of OpenAI and one of the main people behind reinforcement learning from human feedback. He is now chief scientist at Thinking Machines Lab.

bio: Ajeya Cotra is known for her 'biological anchors' report forecasting when transformative AI might arrive. She also wrote a widely read essay on how AI takeover could happen by default.

name: David Silver
bio: David Silver led the DeepMind teams behind AlphaGo, which beat Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016, and AlphaZero, which taught itself chess, shogi and Go from scratch. His work showed that systems learning from their own experience can exceed human skill. He argues the next era of AI will come from agents learning from experience rather than human data. He now leads the AI startup Ineffable Intelligence and teaches at UCL.

name: Douglas Hofstadter
bio: Douglas Hofstadter wrote the Pulitzer Prize-winning Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), which inspired a generation of AI researchers to think about how minds arise. He now describes humanity as playing with fire with AI.

name: Kyunghyun Cho
role: Machine-learning researcher; co-author of neural attention
bio: Kyunghyun Cho co-authored the 2014 paper with Dzmitry Bahdanau and Yoshua Bengio that introduced the attention mechanism for neural machine translation. He also co-invented the GRU, a simpler recurrent network. Attention later became the central idea of the transformer. He is a professor at NYU and has worked on AI for drug and antibody design.

name: Mark Zuckerberg
role: Co-founder, chairman and CEO of Meta
bio: Mark Zuckerberg co-founded Facebook and runs Meta, which released the open-weight Llama models. In 2025 he set up Meta Superintelligence Labs and spent heavily to recruit top researchers. In a July 2025 letter he said superintelligence was "now in sight" and set Meta's goal as "personal superintelligence" for everyone. He favours broad access to AI over keeping it in a few hands.

name: Murray Shanahan
role: Professor of Cognitive Robotics; principal scientist at Google DeepMind
bio: Murray Shanahan works at the meeting point of AI, neuroscience-inspired cognitive architectures and philosophy of mind; he was a scientific adviser on the film Ex Machina. His 2015 book The Technological Singularity walks through scenarios in which AI improves itself and outpaces humans, and he says we cannot know whether superintelligence would be friendly or hostile. In 2014 he said AI researchers should start thinking about the existential-risk issues raised by Stephen Hawking and others. He has more recently written that LLM chatbots are best seen as role-playing characters, warning against loosely calling them conscious or human-like.

name: Andrew Critch
bio: Andrew Critch leads the Mathematical AI Safety Institute, which builds mathematical foundations for the safety of powerful AI. He spent five years as a research scientist at CHAI in Berkeley.

name: Bill Joy
role: Computer engineer; co-founder of Sun Microsystems
bio: Bill Joy co-founded Sun Microsystems and wrote key parts of BSD Unix before turning to the risks of technology. His April 2000 Wired essay "Why the Future Doesn't Need Us" argued that robotics, genetic engineering and nanotech could make humans an endangered species. Coming from a leading technologist, the warning drew wide attention. He called for limiting the development of the most dangerous technologies.

name: Daniel Gross
role: Entrepreneur and investor; co-founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc.
bio: Daniel Gross co-founded the search startup Cue, led AI efforts at Apple and was a partner at Y Combinator, where he started its AI programme. In June 2024 he co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc. with Ilya Sutskever and Daniel Levy, a lab with the sole goal of building safe superintelligence. He is a prominent investor in AI companies. He later left SSI and was reported to have joined Meta's AI effort in 2025.

name: Daniela Amodei
bio: Daniela Amodei is the president of Anthropic, which she co-founded in 2021 with her brother Dario. Before that she was vice president of safety and policy at OpenAI.

name: Norbert Wiener
bio: Norbert Wiener founded cybernetics, the science of feedback and control in animals and machines. In his 1960 essay "Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation" he warned that a machine we cannot effectively interrupt must be given exactly the purpose we really want. That warning is often cited as the first statement of the AI alignment problem. He also foresaw automation's effects on jobs and society.

quotes.text: If we use, to achieve our purposes, a mechanical agency with whose operation we cannot interfere effectively [...] we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire.

role: Machine-learning researcher; inventor of neural attention
org: Mila / McGill University (adjunct); formerly ServiceNow Research

The paper, written with Kyunghyun Cho and Bengio, became the seed of the transformer three years later. Attention now underpins essentially all large language models. He later led conversational-AI research at ServiceNow and co-developed the StarCoder code models.

name: Jesse Hoogland

name: Richard Ngo

name: Hans Moravec
bio: Hans Moravec is a robotics pioneer at Carnegie Mellon whose books Mind Children (1988) and Robot (1999) predicted that machines would reach human-level intelligence around 2040 and then surpass us. He saw these machines as humanity's "mind children" and successors rather than enemies. He is also known for Moravec's paradox: reasoning is easy for computers while perception and movement are hard. His compute-based forecasts of when AI would match the brain influenced later timeline estimates.

name: Holly Elmore
bio: Holly Elmore is the founder and executive director of PauseAI US, which organises protests and public campaigns for an international pause on frontier AI development. She holds a PhD in evolutionary biology from Harvard and previously worked at Rethink Priorities.

name: I. J. Good
bio: I. J. Good worked with Alan Turing as a codebreaker at Bletchley Park during the Second World War. In his 1965 paper "Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine" he described an "intelligence explosion": a machine smarter than any person could design even better machines. He concluded the first such machine would be the last invention humans need make, if it stayed under control. The idea underlies modern thinking about recursive self-improvement and superintelligence.
warning: The first ultraintelligent machine could be our last invention, if we cannot keep it under control.

quotes.text: Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.
quotes.source: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine, via Wikiquote

name: Alex Krizhevsky
role: Computer scientist; lead author of AlexNet
bio: Alex Krizhevsky built AlexNet with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto. In 2012 it won the ImageNet image-recognition contest by a huge margin, trained on just two consumer GPUs. That result is widely seen as the start of the deep-learning boom that leads to today's frontier AI. Krizhevsky later worked at Google and has kept a very low public profile.
